blocks.title: Radios That Find Their Own Space
blocks.subtitle: Sensing the spectrum, learning and sharing it without harm

blocks.text:
Almost all useful radio spectrum is already assigned to someone. Yet measurements show that, at any place and moment, much of it sits idle. Licences reserve frequencies everywhere and always, while their owners use them only in some places and at some times.

A cognitive radio observes its surroundings, finds the idle frequencies and uses them, and moves away the instant the rightful user returns.

blocks.heading: The cognitive cycle
blocks.text: A cognitive radio repeats a loop. It **senses** which frequencies are occupied, **analyses** the gaps, **decides** which to use and with what power and modulation, then **adapts** its transmission. It keeps listening while it works, and learns from experience which channels tend to be free.

steps.text: **Sense.** The radio measures the band to detect signals from licensed users, even very weak ones.
**Analyse.** It estimates how long each gap is likely to last and how good each channel would be.
**Decide.** It selects a channel and transmission settings that meet its needs without disturbing others.
**Adapt.** It transmits, keeps monitoring and hops elsewhere when a licensed user appears.

blocks.heading: The hidden-user problem
blocks.text: A radio in a valley may hear nothing on a channel while a licensed receiver nearby is trying to listen to a distant transmitter. If the cognitive radio transmits, it causes interference it cannot detect. Solutions include **cooperative sensing**, where several radios pool their observations, and **geolocation databases**, which tell a device what channels are free at its position.

items.title: Primary user
items.text: The licence holder, who must be protected from interference.

items.title: Secondary user
items.text: A radio allowed to use spectrum only while the primary user is absent.

items.title: Spectrum hole
items.text: A band assigned to a primary user but unused at a given time and place.

blocks.text: Spectrum is scarce on paper and plentiful in practice. Cognitive radio is the attempt to close that gap.

blocks.heading: Why adoption is gradual
blocks.text: Licence holders must be convinced that sharing will not harm their services. Sensing weak signals reliably is technically demanding, and mistakes cause real interference. Regulators need ways to certify radios whose behaviour is decided by software and, increasingly, by machine learning that is hard to audit.

blocks.question: What must a secondary user do when a primary user starts transmitting?
blocks.explanation: Protection of the licensed user is the first rule of opportunistic access.

blocks.question: Why is cooperative sensing used?
options: To overcome shadowing that hides a primary user from a single radio
blocks.explanation: Pooling observations from several positions reduces the chance of missing a primary signal.

blocks.heading: Key terms and next steps
blocks.text:
**White space**: unused spectrum between active channels. **Sensing threshold**: the level above which a channel is judged occupied. **False alarm / missed detection**: the two kinds of sensing error. **Underlay / overlay**: sharing by staying below an interference limit, or by using gaps. **Policy engine**: software that enforces regulatory rules.
